title: Mini-Whiteboard + Exam Paper
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton describes a weekly Year 11 routine in which students attempt the opening questions of a GCSE paper in silence and the teacher then goes through the answers using mini-whiteboards rather than a passive tick-and-correct. He is sceptical of the usual version, in which a few volunteers answer and the rest copy down the solution, because it looks like learning but may inhibit it. His alternative has every student show an answer to a stream of small questions, such as writing a likely wrong answer or responding to a What if? variation. The move is to turn exam-paper review into continuous whole-class checking for understanding. He then sets out how to respond depending on whether few or some students are correct, using explanation, Call and Respond, Turn and Talk and a re-check question. A generic bank of questions is supplied for any exam question.
points: Reviewing exam papers by hearing from one or two volunteers risks treating a confident student as the benchmark for the whole class; mini-whiteboards expose every response.
Each exam question can be unpacked through varied prompts (write a wrong answer, which calculation first, another correct answer) so students stay actively involved.
The response depends on the board: if few are right, explain clearly then check listening and re-check; if some are right, use Turn and Talk, let students change answers, then tidy up.
What if? questions apply Variation Theory by changing one thing at a time, and the quick-edit mini-whiteboard suits this well.
The extra interactivity costs lesson time but is judged more beneficial than students copying down a solution they do not understand.
quotes: I have seen (and delivered!) far too many lessons like this, where students have a go at questions they can do, leave out ones they can’t, and then passively tick, correct, or copy down the solution (in purple or green pen, of course!) as the teacher goes through it.

Well, if we only get responses from one or two students per question - as is typically the case when going through an exam paper - then we are running a big risk in assuming their understanding is representative of the rest of the class. This problem is exacerbated if we call for volunteers, and take the response of a confident, high-attaining student as our benchmark.
Notice how much useful information the teacher could gain from asking these questions and gathering responses from all students. Notice how actively involved in the process the students have to be.

Call and Respond is my go-to here, getting students to repeat back in unison sections of the explanation we have just given. Finally, in order to determine if our explanation has had any impact, we need to re-check for understanding.

Giving students an opportunity to then stick or change their answers on their mini-whiteboard gives us a good indication that understanding is moving in the right direction. A nice thing to do next is to invite someone who changed their answer to share their reasoning, before we tidy things up with a clear and concise explanation.
These two interventions take time. However, they will be far more beneficial for students’ understanding than copying down a solution from the board that they do not understand.

It allows us to use a key principle from Variation Theory: changing just one thing, holding all else constant, thus drawing students’ attention to what has changed and the effect it has upon the answer.
